item.title: Sayeed Khokon placed on 7-day remand in teenager murder case
item.description:
A Dhaka court has placed former Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) mayor Sayeed Khokon on a seven-day remand for questioning in a case filed over the murder of teenager Abdul Motaleb in the capital’s Dhanmondi area.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mehedi Hasan passed the order on Tuesday, following a petition filed by the investigation officer.
Inspector Sujan Haque of the Detective Branch (DB) police’s Ramna Zonal Team, who is investigating the case, had sought a 10-day remand for Khokon.
Dhaka Metropolitan Public Prosecutor Omar Faruq Faruqi argued in favour of the remand on behalf of the state, while senior lawyer Abu Sayeed Sagor, representing Khokon, opposed the plea and sought his bail.
According to the case statement, Motaleb was shot dead on August 4, 2024 while taking part in a procession near Zigatola Bus Stand during the July uprising.
On August 26, 2024, following the fall of the Awami League government, his father Abdul Matin filed a murder case with Dhanmondi Police Station.
The case names 176 people, including ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina, former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal and former road transport and bridges minister Obaidul Quader. Khokon is listed as the 29th accused in the FIR.
Khokon, son of former undivided Dhaka City Corporation mayor Mohammad Hanif, was elected DSCC mayor in 2015. He was denied the Awami League's nomination in the subsequent mayoral election.
He later contested the 12th parliamentary election with the party's nomination and was elected MP from the Dhaka-6 constituency.
He was detained from a residence in Baridhara around 7am on Tuesday. SRB later handed him over to the Detective Branch (DB) of police.

item.title: NCC Bank to finance export-oriented frozen food sector
item.description:
NCC Bank PLC has signed a participation agreement with Bangladesh Bank under its Tk2,000 crore pre-finance fund for the export-oriented frozen food sector, to promote the country's frozen food industry, diversify exports, and expand financing facilities for entrepreneurs engaged in this sector.
In the presence of Arief Hossain Khan, executive director of Bangladesh Bank, Md Zakir Anam, additional managing director of NCC Bank, and AKM Sayduzzaman, director of Bangladesh Bank, signed and exchanged the agreement on behalf of their respective organizations.
Among others, Muhammad Ansarul Kabir, additional director of Bangladesh Bank; Ahsan Tariq, SEVP and head of RMG & export cell of NCC Bank; and Mohammed Abul Kalam Azad, VP of rmg & export cell of NCC Bank, along with senior officials from both organizations, were present at the event.
The export-oriented frozen food industry is one of the country's promising sectors, offering significant opportunities to expand exports of frozen shrimp, fish, fishery products, and other frozen food items in international markets.
To ensure necessary financial support for entrepreneurs and facilitate production and business operations in this sector, Bangladesh Bank has established the Tk2,000 crore pre-finance fund from its own resources.
Under this fund, eligible entrepreneurs and export-oriented enterprises will receive financing facilities for the production, procurement, processing, and preservation of frozen shrimp, fish, fishery products, and other frozen food items intended for export.
The eligible financing areas include procurement of raw materials, establishment, expansion and modernization of processing plants, purchase of necessary machinery and equipment, construction of cold storage facilities, reopening of closed or partially operational processing plants, and installation of solar power projects to support production and preservation activities.

item.title: Two shot in Khulna amid joint forces' operations
item.description:
Two people, including a shrimp farm owner, were injured in a shooting by unidentified assailants in Khulna on Tuesday night, amid joint forces' operations to curb terrorism.
The incident took place around 9:30pm in the Burir Bhita area under Aranghata Police Station in the metropolitan city.
The injured shrimp farm owner was identified as Solaiman Fakir, also known as Solai, aged over 60.
The assailants opened fire on him, hitting him in the legs, hands and neck. As they fled, they fired another shot, injuring a van driver named Khalek.
Officer-in-Charge (Investigation) of Aranghata Police Station Md Monirul Islam said both victims were rescued by local residents and taken to Khulna Medical College Hospital.
He said the assailants targeted the shrimp farm owner around 9:30pm.
Monirul added that joint forces were conducting security operations in the area, as in other parts of the city, and police had stepped up raids to arrest criminals.
"Efforts are underway to identify and apprehend those involved in the shooting," he said.

item.title: Wife claims physically disabled man framed in Jessore court blast case
item.description:
A man accused in a case filed over a cocktail explosion on the Jessore court premises is physically unfit and unable to walk properly, his wife has claimed, alleging that he was implicated in the case to harass him despite having no involvement in political activities.
Rani Begum made the allegations at a press conference at Press Club Jessore around noon on Tuesday, where she read out a written statement on behalf of her husband, Jahidul Islam Tanvir.
She called for an impartial investigation into the incident, consideration of her husband's physical condition and medical needs, and security for their family.
According to the written statement, Tanvir runs a small fish business beside the Chanchra-Bablatala road to support his family and has no affiliation with any political party.
Rani alleged that after August 5, 2025, members of a force detained and beat her husband in front of their home over an incident. He and his mother were later taken to a police station but were released as no specific evidence was found against him.
She said Tanvir fell into a ditch around 1:30am on October 14 while heading out for his fish business, tearing the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) in his left leg. Following medical advice, he has been unable to move around normally.
The family has also been unable to arrange the necessary treatment due to financial constraints, she added.
However, Tanvir was named among 21 accused in a case filed over the cocktail explosions on theJessore court premises on November 12.
Questioning how a person unable to stand properly could have been involved in the incident, Rani demanded an impartial investigation into the allegations against her husband.
She said Tanvir is the family's sole breadwinner and that they have two sons. His illness, mounting medical expenses and the case have plunged the family into uncertainty.
Those present at the press conference included Tanvir's mother, Jesmin Sultana; aunt, Rekha Begum; another relative, Oheda Begum; neighbour Lamia Sultana; and his seven-year-old son, Taiyan Rahman.
The family also urged the authorities to identify the actual perpetrators and ensure their safety.
Meanwhile, police sources said Tanvir was arrested in connection with a drug-related case filed at a police station in 2023.

RMG factory owners have 'no money,' workers can’t afford food, what’s the solution?
item.description:
Nasima Akhter, a sewing machine operator in Nishchintapur, Ashulia, earns Tk 14,500 at the end of each month. She has a family of six to support.

Her second son was supposed to sit for his SSC examinations this year. But the family could not afford the examination registration fees, so he could not sit for the exams. 

During the same week, the managing director of a garment industry group said that, under the current circumstances, “not a single factory owner has the capacity to increase wages by even one taka.”

Factory owners say they have no money; workers say they cannot make ends meet. The problem is that both are telling the truth.

And sitting comfortably between these two truths, with a quiet smile, is someone who is neither on the streets nor at the wage board—and does not even live in this country: the foreign buyer.

After workers blocked roads from Mirpur to Gazipur demanding a monthly wage of Tk 30,000, the Minimum Wage Board was formed on 1 November.

At its second meeting on 9 November, the workers' representatives submitted a written demand for Tk 32,000—a 156 per cent increase over their current wages.

Workers also took to the streets in 2023 demanding higher wages. Four workers were killed, and more than 70 factories were vandalised.

At the time, the Wage Board increased the minimum wage by 56 per cent, raising it to Tk 12,500. But the workers had demanded Tk 23,000.

Let's assume the board raises wages by 50 to 70 percent this time. Monthly wages would then stand at Tk 18,750 to Tk 21,250—still Tk 11,000 to Tk 13,000 below the workers' demand. That gap is where the fuel for the next explosion is accumulating.

Inequality has added fuel to the workers' anger. Under the new pay scale, the basic salaries of government employees are set to nearly double, while private-sector employees do not even receive a 10 per cent annual increase

So let's make this clear from the outset: this is not a bargaining dispute between factory owners and workers; it is an illness of the economy. And police batons or wage board meetings are no cure for an ailing economy. If you cut off someone's head to cure a headache, the pain may indeed disappear—but so does the person.

Why is the danger greater this time?

This time, four pressures have converged simultaneously.

First, inflation. Poor economic management, printing money to finance government borrowing, and the Iran war have all contributed to soaring prices.

Diesel prices alone have risen from Tk 100 to Tk 135 per litre this year. According to the IMF's forecast, average inflation in the current fiscal year will be around 11 percent. The wages set in 2023 cannot sustain workers in the 2026 marketplace.

Second, a weakening economy. According to provisional Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) figures, private investment as a share of GDP stood at just 21.53 percent in the last fiscal year—the lowest level in 14 years.

The IMF forecasts economic growth of only 3.2 percent, lower than during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Third, pressure on the informal sector. Pavement shops and easy-bikes (battery-powered three-wheelers) served as an unofficial safety net for people who had lost their jobs. Evictions are tearing that safety net apart, and angry street vendors are now joining workers' marches.

Fourth, politics. Ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has announced that she will return in December. And there is no shortage of people looking to fish in troubled waters.

But these are merely sparks. The real stockpile of gunpowder has been accumulating inside the industry itself.

Selling cheap, yet finding no buyers

Trump's tariffs on China could have been a lottery ticket for us. In February, we even overtook China to become the second-largest exporter to the US market.

But in August, despite carrying the burden of steep tariffs, China overtook us again.

According to OTEXA data, Bangladesh's exports to the United States fell by 4.57 per cent between January and September, amounting to $6.14 billion.

Cambodia's exports increased by more than 6 percent, while Vietnam managed to retain its market share despite raising prices. The setback in Europe has been even greater. China, having faced difficulties in the US market, has made an aggressive push into Europe.

Between January and August, Bangladesh recorded the highest rate of export decline to Europe among all countries. The extent of that decline was discussed in this very newspaper last week in an article titled Three Houses on the Same Street.

During the same period, China's exports to Europe actually increased by 2.38 percent. Prices are also falling. Our garments fetch €13.76 per kilogram in Europe, compared with €19.82 for Chinese products.

While our competitors are raising their prices, we cannot maintain export volumes even by selling more cheaply. Exports to the US have declined by 3.65 per cent.

It is like a shopkeeper at a marketplace who offers the lowest price of all but still cannot find customers.

Even loss-making factories cannot afford to close

More than 2,000 factories are competing for a shrinking pool of orders. Many manufacturers have concluded that taking orders at a loss is better than leaving their machines idle. On that calculation, some are accepting orders at prices below their production costs.

Who pockets the profit? Research by Public Eye and the Clean Clothes Campaign shows that Bangladesh accounts for 61 percent of the cotton T-shirts imported into Europe.

In 2025, the average price of these T-shirts in Europe was $2.67, while Bangladeshi T-shirts fetched just $2.06.

Taking inflation into account, brands now buy T-shirts at nearly half the price they paid 25 years ago. Yet workers' wages account for only 12 percent of that price.

According to our straightforward calculations, even doubling workers' wages would increase the production cost by only about 25 cents per T-shirt. The same T-shirt sells in retail stores for between $12 and $20.

In a healthy market, loss-making factories shut down. Here, however, closing a factory is the most expensive option.

Take Beximco, for example. Following the closure of 14 factories, outstanding dues to 33,244 workers amounted to Tk 525 crore—more than Tk 150,000 per worker. Ultimately, the government had to settle those payments.

Even an ordinary factory employing 10,000 workers faces legal liabilities exceeding Tk 75 crore when it closes. On top of that, there are rescheduled loans: the moment a factory shuts down, it risks being classified as a loan defaulter.

That is why factories continue operating despite mounting losses, until they finally run out of steam.

According to Industrial Police data, 457 industrial establishments have permanently closed over the past two years, including 170 textile and garment factories.

The garment sector alone has seen approximately 150,000 workers lose their jobs.

Dollars disappearing from workers' pockets

In December 2023, a monthly wage of Tk 12,500 was worth $113. Today, it is worth just $101. The figure in taka remains the same, yet $12 has disappeared from workers' pockets in just three years.

Lucky, an operator in Gazipur, earns Tk 21,900 a month, including overtime, but still has to borrow money every month to make ends meet.

Why are even machine operators joining the protests? Because the minimum wage is the first step on the wage ladder; when that step moves, every other step moves with it.

One factory owner has even included landlords on his list of those allegedly instigating the protests.

The reason? Whenever wages go up, rents go up the very next day. Don't laugh—the statement is not entirely untrue.

According to H&M, Bangladesh's seven competing countries, including China and Vietnam, all have higher minimum wages than ours.

Cambodia's minimum wage this year is $210—more than double ours—yet the country is still managing to raise its prices in the European market. Cheap labour is no longer our trump card.

Inequality has added fuel to the workers' anger. Under the new pay scale, the basic salaries of government employees are set to nearly double, while private-sector employees do not even receive a 10 per cent annual increase.

Then, in May, another Tk 600 billion in incentives was announced, with the government covering 6 percent of the interest. There have been instances of such benefits being misused in the past as well.

CPD proposes Tk 18,578–Tk 24,204 wage range for garment workers

Seven proposals for the government

The cure for an ailing economy must come from within the economy itself. The government does not have the financial capacity to subsidize the industry indefinitely. So there are two possible ways forward: increase income and reduce costs.

1. Gradually adjust the value of the taka

Factory owners are telling us that if the dollar rises from its current rate of Tk 124 to Tk 130 or Tk 135, they will be able to pay a minimum monthly wage of Tk 25,000.

Consider a factory that exports $1 million worth of goods every month. If half of its earnings go towards raw materials, the remaining $500,000, converted at Tk 135 per dollar, would generate approximately Tk 5.3 million in additional monthly revenue.

However, this would also increase foreign loan repayment costs and inflation. Therefore, any adjustment should be gradual and controlled. Currency depreciation can help, but it cannot be the sole source of funding higher wages.

2. Break down the artificial barriers in the yarn market

Three restrictions have created a protected market for a handful of influential spinning mills:

·         A ban on yarn imports through land ports.

·         Requiring bank guarantees instead of bonded warehouse facilities for yarn in the 10-to-30-count range.

·         A directive requiring manufacturers to purchase half of their yarn from domestic mills.

The price of 30-count yarn has already increased by around 15 cents per kilogram.

For a knitwear factory requiring 100 tonnes of yarn a month, this translates into an additional monthly cost of approximately Tk 1.85 million—equivalent to the current wages of 150 workers.

Tear down these barriers, but strengthen monitoring to prevent bonded yarn from being diverted into the open market.

The real problems facing spinning mills are gas shortages and high interest rates. The remedies should target those problems directly.

3. Prioritise energy supply to industrial zones

Fuel and electricity should be prioritized for industrial areas. Due to shortages of gas and electricity, many factories are forced to run on diesel.

According to a simple calculation by an engineer, if a generator produces 3.5 units of electricity per litre of diesel, the fuel cost alone comes to approximately Tk 38 per unit. By comparison, grid electricity for industrial consumers costs around Tk 14 per unit.

Reducing this cost could translate directly into higher wages for workers.

4. Resolve the banking sector's bottlenecks

In September, private-sector credit growth stood at just 4.17 percent, the lowest in three decades.

A special mechanism for loan restructuring should be introduced through the sale or merger of businesses. Factories should be allowed to pass into financially stronger hands while jobs are preserved.

5. Stop extortion on the streets and bribery behind desks

Factory owners have to pay money in two places: on the streets and across office desks.

Last week's article included a basic calculation of these two forms of extortion. The situation in the garment sector is even more striking.

Extortion on the streets does not disappear when the government changes; only the beneficiaries change. One factory in Tongi was forced to sell Tk 5 million worth of monthly garment waste (jhut) at half its market price. In effect, the extortionists pocketed an amount equivalent to the wages of 200 workers.

At a meeting of the National Board of Revenue (NBR), the president of the Terry Towel Exporters Association went so far as to say: “Stop bribery, and we will never ask for tax reductions again.”

Interestingly, this is one issue on which both sides agree.

On 3 November, an organisation representing workers also stated that eliminating bribery at ports and extortion in transportation would reduce factory owners' costs substantially, making wage increases easier to implement.

This does not require a budget. It requires political will.

6. Annual wage adjustments, with buyers sharing the cost

Wages should be adjusted every year, and buyers should also share the cost.

Based on the average inflation rate over the past three years, if wages had been adjusted annually by 9.5 percent, the minimum wage of Tk 12,500 would have automatically risen to approximately Tk 16,400 by now.

Under the amended Labour Act, wage reviews are currently conducted every three years. Cambodia, by contrast, reviews wages annually.

The irony is that in 2023, 15 American brands wrote to the Prime Minister recommending annual wage reviews, alongside a commitment to “responsible purchasing practices.”

Yet garment prices are moving in the opposite direction—they are falling.

With that letter in hand, the government and BGMEA should secure a commitment from buyers to incorporate the cost of new wages into their purchasing prices.

7. Avoid confrontation at all costs

In 2023, blanket cases were filed against 11,000 workers. That did not put out the fire.

This time, in just five cases filed in Mirpur, approximately 11,500 unidentified individuals have been named as accused.

Those responsible for sabotage should be arrested. But branding the entire movement as an Awami League agenda will only alienate genuinely angry workers.

Nasima is not an agent of any political party. She simply could not afford the money needed to register her son for his examinations.

In the long run: Fewer factories, stronger factories

Does Bangladesh really need more than 2,000 garment factories?

Through mergers, a smaller number of larger factories could gain greater bargaining power, spread fixed costs across higher production volumes, invest in technology and move into higher-value products made from synthetic fibres.

Synthetic fibres now account for half of global garment trade. According to PwC, they make up just 27 per cent of Bangladesh's exports, compared with 56 per cent for Vietnam and 62 per cent for China.

To achieve this, we need a clear exit policy that allows factory owners to leave the business at a lower cost after settling workers' dues.

Thousands of our factories survive not because they are efficient, but because they cannot afford to shut down.

In economic terms, these are called “zombie firms”: businesses that refuse to die even when they are effectively dead, while also dragging down the competitiveness of healthier factories around them.

Making room for efficient businesses by allowing such firms to exit is known as “creative destruction”—a concept explained by Nobel laureates Philippe Aghion, Peter Howitt and Joel Mokyr, who received the Nobel Prize in Economics last year.

However, if the cost of this destruction is placed entirely on workers' shoulders, it will no longer be creative.

An effective exit policy must also include unemployment benefits and retraining programmes for displaced workers.

No painless way forward

Every option comes at a cost—higher inflation, political pressure, and the loss of some jobs.

But the biggest mistake would be to treat an economic illness as a law-and-order problem and simply wait for the next explosion.

If we stop after deciding on a new minimum wage figure, we will find ourselves back at the same barricades three years from now, with an even weaker industry.

The garment industry accounts for more than 80 per cent of Bangladesh's exports and keeps the kitchens of millions of families running. What it needs is not blame, but sound calculations.

And the calculation is not complicated. The government must stop extortion on the streets and bribery across office desks, factory owners must become more efficient, and buyers must pay that additional 25 cents per T-shirt.

Otherwise, the foreign buyers' knowing smiles will not disappear. Only our factories will.

* Fahim Mashroor is the founder of BDjobs.com.

* Subail Bin Alam is an engineer-economist and a columnist on sustainable development. Email: contact@subail.com

item.title: Rise Above All 10X set to take place on 27 November at KIB
item.description:
After nine editions, more than 21,500 in-person attendees, over 1,550 pieces of content, and more than 100 million views and engagements online, Rise Above All—Bangladesh's largest public speaking platform, is back for its milestone tenth edition.

‘Mastercard Presents Rise Above All 10X, Powered by MTB’ will take place on Friday, 27 November 2026, from 09:00 am to 9:00 pm at the Krishibid Institution Bangladesh (KIB) Complex, Khamarbari, Dhaka, reports a press release.  

Organised by Don Sumdany Facilitation & Consultancy in association with Fit Elegance, with United Aygaz as energy partner, Shwapno as strategic partner and Bata as musical partner, this landmark edition comes under the theme ‘10 Years of Rise. 10X Your Growth’.

This year's stage will bring together some of the country's top leaders from banking, finance, healthcare and manufacturing, alongside familiar faces from entertainment.

Confirmed speakers include Zakia Sultana, country manager of Mastercard Bangladesh; Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director and CEO of Mutual Trust Bank PLC (MTB); Faria Yasmin, managing director of Bata Bangladesh; Aameir Alihussain, managing director of BSRM Group; and Muhit Rahman, chief executive officer of ONE Bank PLC.

The list also include Tasneem Sinha, managing director of The ACME Laboratories Ltd; Humaira Azam, managing director of LankaBangla Finance PLC; Sayef Nasir, managing director of SMC Enterprise Limited; and Rubaba Dowla, country managing director of Oracle Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

Harun Ortaç, chief executive officer of United Aygaz LPG, will become the first expatriate speaker to take the Rise Above All stage. Actors Tawsif Mahbub and Sabila Nur are also expected to attend while more names will be announced in the coming days.

The speakers will share their career journeys, including the setbacks along the way, and take part in interactive sessions with the audience. The day will wrap up with a live performance by Warfaze.
At its heart, Rise Above All has always been about people. Over the past decade, it has helped students and young professionals find direction, believe in themselves and take the next step in their careers and lives.

For many attendees, it is a rare chance to hear extraordinary achievers speak directly about their struggles and turning points, not from a screen or a headline, but face to face.

Many who first came as students have returned years later as professionals, entrepreneurs and leaders in their own right. The event also gives visitors the opportunity to experience and interact with a wide range of brands throughout the day.

For the tenth edition, United Healthcare, Polar Ice Cream, Kool, Aqua Paints, SMC Plus, OPPO and Sheltech are co-sponsoring the event.

Other partners include Turkish Airlines, Elite Steel, Coca-Cola, KFC, Foodi, Chery, Prothom Alo, The Daily Star, Channel i, Dan Cake, Fresh, Bombay Sweets, AMA Coffee, Senora, Dettol, Blucheez, Tabaq Coffee, ISHO, Tickify, ICE Today, Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport, Shutter Lens, Elite Force and Link3.

The organisers thanked all partners for standing alongside Rise Above All as it celebrates its tenth edition. Tickets are available on Tickify.

item.title: Police vehicle set on fire, bomb-like object recovered on highway in Gazipur
item.description:
Amid heightened tensions in Gazipur over a workers’ movement, miscreants set fire to a police vehicle and authorities recovered a bomb-like object.

The incident involving the police vehicle took place at around 10:15 am on Wednesday in the Chhaidana area of the Dhaka–Mymensingh Highway.

Earlier, on Tuesday evening, people spotted a red bomb-like object lying on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway beside the Konabari Flyover. A bomb disposal team later neutralised it.

Police officer’s vehicle set on fire

Miscreants set fire to a police vehicle beside the house of former Gazipur City Corporation Mayor Jahangir Alam in the Chhaidana area of the Dhaka–Mymensingh Highway. The incident took place at around 10:15 am today, Wednesday.

Mohammad Mohiuddin Ahmed, deputy commissioner of the Gazipur Metropolitan Police, used the vehicle. He serves as Deputy Commissioner (Crime–South Division) and also holds additional responsibility as Deputy Commissioner (Estate and Development).

According to police and Fire Service sources, a workers’ movement had been underway in the Chhaidana area of Gazipur city since the morning. After receiving news of the protest, Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Mohiuddin Ahmed was heading there. When he reached an area beside former mayor Jahangir Alam’s house, several miscreants carrying sticks and other weapons blocked the police vehicle. They then vandalised the vehicle and eventually set it on fire.

After receiving the report, firefighters from the Chandana Chowrasta Modern Fire Service Station in Gazipur rushed to the scene and brought the fire under control.

Hiron Mia, an official at the fire service station, said, "After receiving the information, two of our units rushed to the scene and brought the fire under control."

Confirming that the vehicle belonged to the Gazipur Metropolitan Police, Amzad Hossain, superintendent of police of the Gazipur Industrial Police said, "Miscreants set fire to the vehicle."

Bomb-like object bears the inscription “Warning: Explosion”

Panic spread among local residents after they spotted a red bomb-like object lying in Konabari, within Gazipur city. They found it on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway, on the eastern side of the Konabari Flyover, after Tuesday evening. They subsequently informed the police.

According to police and local sources, the object looked much like a bomb or cocktail. Its outer casing resembled a red bowl, with wires protruding from it. The words ‘Warning Explosive’ appeared on the red casing, with “MK.” written underneath.

The unusual object attracted a crowd of curious onlookers, who gathered on the pavement nearby. This sparked panic in the area.

After receiving the information, police cordoned off the scene and called in a bomb disposal team to examine the object.

Iftekhar Hossain, officer-in-charge (OC) of Konabari police station, confirmed the incident.

5 of travel vlogger Nadir’s favourite dishes from around the world
item.description:
Nadir Nibras is a Bangladeshi travel vlogger who has gained popularity for his travel videos under the name ‘Nadir On The Go’. He spends the entire year travelling from one country to another. Jhalmuri and fuchka are among his favourite Bangladeshi street foods. 

However, we wanted to find out which dishes from around the world have made it on to his list of favourites. Speaking to us over WhatsApp from Serbia, Nadir shared the names of five dishes he particularly enjoys. Even now, recalling the taste of these dishes is enough to make his mouth water. He says:

1. Rice burrito

I used to eat rice burrito bowls almost every day when I visited Chipotle, an American restaurant chain. You can mix and match various ingredients in the bowl. I would have mine with rice, chicken, guacamole, cheese, beans and sour cream.

2. Tacos

The second dish is Mexican tacos, which I consider one of the best foods in the world. They come with various kinds of fish or meat. My favourite, however, is taco de pollo, made with chicken. You can customise it and make it just the way you like.

3. Khao soi

My third choice is a dish from northern Thailand called khao soi. It is a type of noodle soup, served with a delicious, mildly spicy coconut-based curry. It contains both boiled and crispy fried noodles.

4. Ćevapi

The fourth dish is ćevapi, which I had in Bosnia. It is a popular meat dish across the Balkans and essentially consists of grilled meat. It is usually made with beef or lamb and served with a little salad. It is absolutely delicious, too.

5. Kuru fasulye

Finally, there is the Turkish dish kuru fasulye. It is made with a type of red bean and is usually eaten with pilaf and chilli. I spent almost five months in Türkiye, and I lost count of how many times I ate kuru fasulye during that period.

item.title: 2 buses torched in Pirojpur, helper found dead inside one
item.description:
Two buses were set on fire in Bhandaria upazila of Pirojpur early Wednesday. A bus helper who was asleep inside one of the vehicles was burnt to death in the incident. 

The fires broke out at Bhandaria Bus Stand at around 4:00 am.

The deceased was identified as Siam, 25, son of Kabir Hossain of Idilkathi village in Babuganj upazila of Barishal.

According to Bhandaria police, miscreants set fire to two buses parked at the bus stand, belonging to Bahak Paribahan and Lisa Paribahan. Fire service personnel rushed to the scene after being alerted and brought the fires under control. Siam’s burnt body was later recovered from inside the Bahak Paribahan bus.

Bhandaria police station Officer-in-Charge Dewan Jaglul Hasan said the body would be sent to hospital for an autopsy.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said no member of Siam’s family had contacted the police. Nor had the bus owners filed any complaint. 

“If a complaint is lodged, legal action will be taken following an investigation,” he added.

item.title: Govt calls bribery ‘gifts’, extortion ‘settlements’: Hasnat Abdullah
item.description:
Hasnat Abdullah, a Member of Parliament from the National Citizen Party (NCP), has said that the government refers to bribes as “gifts”, extortion as “settlements” and loan defaulters as “indebted”.

Accusing the government of concealing reality through word play, he said ready-made garment factory owners were leading miserable lives as they continued to provide so-called gifts to various government offices and influential individuals. Yet the responsibility for increasing workers’ wages was being placed solely on the owners.

Speaking during a discussion on the crisis in the garment industry in Parliament on Tuesday, the opposition MP criticised the government’s management, the business environment, corruption and the energy situation.

He said, “‘If workers cannot survive and industries cannot survive, the country cannot survive’—both the government and the opposition believe this. But the question is, if the government itself creates obstacles to doing business, how can industries survive?”

Hasnat Abdullah further said inflation had increased by more than 26 per cent cumulatively over the past three years. A family of four in Dhaka spends Tk 12,000 to Tk 16,000 a month on food, while the minimum wage for garment workers stands at Tk 12,000. Under these circumstances, workers are finding it increasingly difficult to make ends meet. In addition to high food prices, rising gas prices and the fuel crisis have further aggravated their hardship.

Referring to a speech by State Minister for Planning Zonayed Saki in Parliament, Hasnat Abdullah said that Saki had pledged to set the national minimum wage at Tk 20,000 if his party came to power. They had expected to see this commitment reflected in the activities of the wage board, but the board was not even holding its meetings regularly.

He described the workers’ protests as justified and alleged that the government was failing to manage the situation properly.

Highlighting the difficulties faced by garment factory owners, Hasnat said, “Almost all the raw materials required by the garment industry have to be imported from abroad. From the import of these raw materials to port operations, bonded warehouses, factories and exports, owners have to obtain approval from multiple government offices at different stages. At every stage, they have to provide so-called ‘gifts’.”

Referring to George Orwell’s novel, the opposition MP went on to make a sarcastic remark, saying, “This cannot be called bribery; it has to be called a gift. In exactly the same way, this government has successfully adopted George Orwell’s formula. What this government has done is that they do not call loan defaulters ‘loan defaulters’; they call them ‘indebted’. They do not call extortion ‘extortion’; they call it ‘settlement’. And they do not call bribes ‘bribes’; what do they call them? ‘Gifts’. The burden of these gifts has become so unbearable that garment factory owners today are leading miserable lives as they continue to provide them.”

Hasnat alleged that factory owners were also harassed under the pretext of factory inspections.

He said they also had to pay government party leaders or influential individuals by appointing them as consultants to ensure business security, a practice known as “protection money”. In addition, businesses were asked to pay money through various institutions, including Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) offices and the police, under the pretext of government events such as 26 March, 16 December and Pahela Boishakh.

He described these collections as “government extortion”.

Calling for a more business-friendly operating environment, the NCP MP said, “The government does not pay workers’ salaries; the factory owners have to pay them. Therefore, the government’s responsibility is to make doing business easier, reduce production costs and create a business-friendly environment. Instead of fulfilling this role, however, the government is creating more obstacles for businesses.”

He alleged that although the government was not directly involved in these activities, it was allowing them to continue through its inaction.

Hasnat Abdullah also criticised the government over the gas crisis. He said, “We are not saying that the government bombed Iran and caused the gas crisis. However, the crisis is being exploited to create opportunities for corruption.”

Referring to a proposal to establish a third LNG regasification terminal, he questioned the initiative, which would cost more than Tk 63 billion (6,300 crore).

He also alleged that the State Minister had failed to answer his question about the connection between the project and a proposal made by a grandson of a Member of Parliament.

Highlighting the link between the garment industry crisis and political instability, Hasnat said they had found evidence of the Awami League's involvement in the movement.

He said the government must take responsibility for preventing such involvement and acts of sabotage.

He also alleged that the Awami League was attempting to destabilise the situation in Bangladesh by using Indian territory.

According to him, if instability and acts of arson and sabotage continued across the country, from Gopalganj to other areas, no sector, including the garment industry, would be able to survive.

NCP leader Hasnat Abdullah further said that Bangladesh must protect workers’ interests, ensure a favourable business environment for factory owners and maintain stability in the country to retain its US$45 billion garment export market.

He also claimed that, during the current order season, most orders placed with Bangladesh were beginning to shift to India.

He warned that if this situation continued, the country's employment crisis would worsen further.

Calling on the government and opposition to work together to resolve the crisis, Hasnat said wages must be adjusted in line with workers’ cost of living.

At the same time, he said, unnecessary expenses, harassment and extortion imposed on business owners must be reduced.

Hasnat Abdullah also called for those involved in and financing such conspiracies on behalf of the Awami League to be identified and brought to justice.
