item.title: Garment workers, BNP activists clash in Mirpur
item.description:
Garment workers clashed with local BNP activists in Kafrul, Mirpur, on Wednesday morning over allegations that several female workers had been harassed.
The incident took place around 9am near Load Star Fashion and Mid Asia Fashion factories in Mirpur-13, with both sides chasing each other and exchanging brickbats.
Police fired around 10 sound grenades to bring the situation under control.
Agitated workers also vandalized the windows of a Social Islami Bank branch in the Mymensingh Samity building and tore down a banner bearing the photograph of Dhaka North Administrator Md Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton.
According to police, the two factories employ around 5,000 workers. The unrest began after workers alleged that employees of nearby factories had disrupted their production activities and local BNP activists had harassed female workers.
Mirpur Division Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Zahidul Islam said the situation was now under control, with adequate police personnel deployed at the scene.

item.title: Ex-state minister Nazrul Islam Hiru arrested
item.description:
Former state minister for water resources Lt Col (retd) Mohammad Nazrul Islam Hiru has been arrested by the Special Response Battalion (SRB-01).
He was arrested during a raid at his residence in Baridhara DOHS in the capital around 7:30am on Wednesday.
A team led by SRB-01 ASP Lutfar conducted the operation.
Several arrest warrants had been issued against him in multiple cases, including those involving sabotage, according to the report.
Following his arrest, SRB personnel took him to the battalion headquarters in Uttara.
Hiru is a retired military officer, freedom fighter and Awami League politician.
He served as the MP for Narsingdi-1 for four consecutive terms from 2009 to 2024 and as state minister for water resources from 2014 to 2018.

item.title: 44 BGB platoons deployed in four districts amid workers' unrest
item.description:
A total of 44 platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in industrial areas across Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj and Mymensingh to maintain law and order and assist the civil administration amid ongoing workers' unrest.
The BGB media wing shared the information on Wednesday.
Of the deployed personnel, 20 platoons are in Dhaka, covering Mirpur, Hemayetpur, Savar and Ashulia, including Yunus Convention Hall, Kathgara, Jirabo, Hamim Group, Midlar Group and Jamgara.
Another 15 platoons have been deployed in Gazipur, covering Chandra, Polli Bidyut, Mouchak, Konabari, Telirchala, Kashimpur, Bhogra Bypass, Gacha, Salna and Baishya Kuribari.
Seven platoons are stationed in Narayanganj, covering Shibu Market, Katherpul, Jalkuri, the BSCIC Industrial Estate, Chashara Mor, Kanchpur Bridge and Shimrail. The remaining two platoons are deployed in Bhaluka and Trishal in Mymensingh.
The BGB said its personnel were working in coordination with the local administration and police to maintain law and order in the industrial areas.
A monitoring cell at BGB headquarters is also reviewing live footage from drones, body-worn cameras and other specialised equipment to monitor developments, facilitate the exchange of information and coordinate responses, the force said.

item.title: Fire at Sattola slum brought under control
item.description:
A fire at Sattola slum in the capital’s Mohakhali area was brought under control at 11am on Wednesday after eight Fire Service units responded to the blaze.
The fire broke out at around 9:40am, said Anwarul Islam, an official at the Fire Service media cell.
He said eight units were deployed to the scene, including three from Tejgaon Fire Station, two from Baridhara Fire Station and two from Kurmitola Fire Station.
The cause of the fire and the extent of the damage are yet to be determined.

item.title: Workers block Dhaka-Mymensingh highway again amid wage protests
item.description:
Garment workers have again blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway in Gazipur, bringing traffic to a standstill amid ongoing protests demanding higher wages.
The blockade began around 9:45am on Wednesday, when workers from several garment factories in the Chhaydana area of Gazipur city took to the highway at Chhaydana and Hariken, halting traffic in both directions and causing severe disruption for commuters.
Industrial Police, local police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel reached the scene and are engaging with the workers to bring the situation under control.
Meanwhile, workers at SM Knit Wear in the Notun Bazar area of Sreepur, Golden Refit Garments in Bagher Bazar and Fakira Garments in Bhabanipur have stopped work and staged peaceful sit-ins on their factory floors.
In Konabari, workers from two other garment factories also staged protests but did not block the highway.
Amjad Hossain, superintendent of police for the Gazipur industrial zone, said efforts were underway to bring the situation under control.
He said 10 factories had declared a holiday on Wednesday amid the workers' unrest, while 39 factories had been closed indefinitely, based on reports received on Tuesday.
According to the Industrial Police, workers in the Gazipur industrial zone have been protesting for several days, demanding an increase in the minimum wage.
On Tuesday, workers staged demonstrations in several areas, including Konabari, Kashimpur, Chandna Chourasta, Jarun, Naojor, Chhaydana, Bhogra, and the C&B-2 and Apada areas of Sreepur.
The protests turned violent, with clashes involving brick-throwing, tear gas and sound grenades. Several people, including police officers, garment workers and journalists, were injured.
To prevent further unrest, authorities ordered the closure of 70 factories across the district from 11:30am on Tuesday.

item.title: Awami League office, ex-MP Bahar's home set on fire again in Comilla
item.description:
The Comilla South district office of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, and the residence and personal office of former MP AKM Bahauddin Bahar were set on fire again on early Wednesday.
The incidents took place around 1am in the Ramghat and Munsef Bari areas of the city. This marks the third time Bahar's residence and political office have been attacked, vandalized and set on fire.
Videos circulating on social media show a group of BNP and its affiliated organisation leaders and activists, led by Comilla South district Swechchhasebak Dal Convener Syed Meraj Uddin, marching to the Awami League office in Ramghat.
They chanted slogans protesting an attack on a police station in Gopalganj and the arson attack on the residence of BNP MP SM Zilani before setting fire outside the party office.
Another video shows a group of youths marching to Bahar's residence in Munsef Bari. They chanted similar slogans before pouring petrol inside the gate of his personal office on the ground floor and setting it on fire. Papers and wooden materials outside the office were also set ablaze.
Syed Meraj Uddin said the attacks in Gopalganj and on the residence of BNP MP SM Zilani were unacceptable. He said they held an impromptu procession demanding the arrest and exemplary punishment of those involved.
Regarding the fire outside the Awami League office, he said some agitated activists had set fire to tyres and papers out of long-standing resentment, but had no intention of causing major damage. He added that the organisation believed in peaceful and democratic movements.
Kotwali Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Touhidul Anwar said the fire did not last long and no one entered the office. A few youths started the fire from outside using paper, he added.
According to local and party sources, the Awami League offices of Comilla South district and metropolitan units in Ramghat were vandalized and set on fire on August 5, 2024, the day the Awami League government fell.
Bahar's residence and personal office were also attacked, vandalized and looted that day. Since then, family members have not stayed there, except for a night guard.
On the night of February 5, 2025, the residence was attacked again. The attackers tried to break the window grilles, threw bricks and stones, vandalized several parts of the house and set fire to several rooms and the front section after pouring petrol on them.
Attempts were also made to attack the Awami League's metropolitan and south district offices in Ramghat that night. The brick structure in front of the south district office's main gate was demolished.
Former MP AKM Bahauddin Bahar, his daughter and former Comilla City Corporation mayor Dr Tahsin Bahar Suchona, and other family members are currently abroad.

item.title: Winter to be 'warm' for Bangladesh this year
item.description:
Bangladesh is set to experience a gradual onset of winter starting next week, with the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) forecasting a 'warm winter' this year due to the effects of El Nino phase.
"We are expecting a warm winter this year due to El Nino phase," meteorologist Dr Muhammad Abul Kalam Mallik told BSS on Tuesday.
The El Nino phase is the warm part of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate cycle that swings between warm and cool states in the tropical Pacific Ocean every two to seven years.
Dr Mallik said the winter is expected to start in the country from next week, while fog has already started forming in remote areas across the country.
However, he predicted that the intensity and duration of severe coldwaves would be relatively low this year.
According to the BMD's seasonal outlook, chilly conditions and light morning fog will begin appearing in the northern, northeastern, and central districts by the third week of November. Winter intensity will build steadily through December before reaching its peak in January 2027, with cold weather expected to linger until mid-February.
Meteorologists projected that four to six mild-to-moderate coldwaves would sweep through various parts of the country this season, driving regional minimum temperatures down between 6 and 10°C.
Additionally, two to three severe cold spells could hit the northwest, northeast, and central regions, potentially pushing mercury levels as low as 4 to 6°C.
In the capital, Dhaka, nighttime and early morning temperatures are expected to dip to between 11 and 13°C at the height of the season.
Forecasters also warned of dense late-night and early-morning fog, particularly in the northern and central river basins. The reduced visibility is expected to cause temporary disruptions to road, river, and air transport networks during peak winter weeks.
While broader regional climate models indicate potential warming influences from El Nino patterns this year, weather officials noted that localised cold snaps and sharp overnight temperature drops will still impact daily life and agriculture across the delta nation.
Noting that El Nino is active, Mallik said that during the winter in Bangladesh, night temperatures, on average, remains 14 to 24°C based on stations. "This season, nighttime temperature will be 1 to 2°C higher."
The meteorologist said sea surface temperature, land surface temperature and ocean heat content capacity have increased this year due to global warming, resulting in rise of overall temperature.
"To address this situation, we need localisation of global knowledge and globalisation of local knowledge," he said. According to the three-month climate outlook issued by the BMD on November 1, day and nighttime temperature may remain higher than normal.
Moderate to dense fog may occur at some places across the country, including river basins, from late night to morning, while light to moderate fog may prevail elsewhere over the country.
Due to dense fog, the difference between day and night temperatures may decrease, which may intensify the feeling of cold.
Four to six mild (08-10øC) to moderate (06-08øC) coldwaves may sweep across parts of the country, of which 2-3 may intensify into severe coldwaves (04-06øC) during the winter, the outlook said.

item.title: Most factories reopen in Gazipur after workers' protests
item.description:
Factory operations have resumed across much of Gazipur's industrial belt following a daylong workers' protest on Tuesday, with most factories reopening on Wednesday morning.
Workers joined their shifts at factories in Bhogra Bypass, Naojor, Konabari, Kashimpur, Chandra, Palli Bidyut road, Bhabanipur, Memberbari, Notun Bazar, and Tongi.
Police maintained surveillance across the industrial areas, with no untoward incidents reported until 9:30am.
On Tuesday, garment workers took to the streets demanding a minimum wage and blocked highways. Clashes broke out between workers and police in Bhogra Bypass and the No 2 C&B and Aspada areas of Sreepur.
The clashes involved brick-throwing, tear gas and sound grenades, leaving several police personnel, workers and journalists injured.
Around 70% of garment factories sent workers home early on Tuesday, while 70 factories declared holidays to prevent further unrest.
On Wednesday, security was tightened across the industrial belt, with Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) members deployed alongside police. Traffic on the Dhaka-Mymensingh and Dhaka-Tangail highways remained normal, and no fresh protests were reported.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Mohammad Amzad Hossain said production had resumed at many factories that were closed on Tuesday.
Workers entered factories peacefully and joined production, with no untoward incidents reported since morning, he said.
He added that members of Gazipur Metropolitan Police, district police, industrial police, BGB, the Special Reserve Battalion (SRB) and Ansar would remain deployed to maintain law and order.

item.title: 21 platoons BGB deployed in Gopalganj
item.description:
A total of 21 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed at key locations across Gopalganj to maintain law and order, ensure public security and tackle any untoward situation.
The BGB media department disclosed the information on Wednesday.
According to the BGB, deployed personnel are working in coordination with the Gopalganj district administration and police.
The BGB headquarters' monitoring cell is also using technology-based surveillance to closely monitor the law and order situation and coordinate field operations.
Live footage from drones, body-worn cameras and improvised devices is being monitored round the clock, the force said.

item.title: Dense fog disrupts ferry services on Paturia-Daulatdia route for 2 hours
item.description:
Ferry services on the Paturia-Daulatdia route were suspended for two hours on Wednesday morning due to dense fog, disrupting river crossings and leaving more than a hundred vehicles stranded at the terminals.
During the suspension, a ferry named Birshreshtha Jahangir remained anchored in the middle of the river, while nine other ferries were berthed at various pontoons at the Paturia and Daulatdia terminals.
BIWTC Deputy General Manager (DGM) Abdus Salam said ferry operations were suspended at 6:00am on Wednesday as dense fog intensified, posing a risk of maritime accidents.
The suspension continued for two hours, with ferry services resuming around 8:00am as visibility improved and the fog began to clear.
Meanwhile, ferry services on the Aricha-Kazirhat route were also suspended for an hour from 6m due to dense fog.

item.title: Parked bus torched in Narayanganj
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to a parked bus in the Sanarpar area of Siddhirganj, Narayanganj, at around 3:30am on Wednesday.
The bus, belonging to Three Star Paribahan, was parked beside the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway near a garage owned by Md Latif when two youths on a motorcycle set it ablaze and fled.
Local residents rushed to the spot and extinguished the fire, which damaged several parts of the bus.
No casualties were reported.
The bus was owned by Lokman Mamun, a resident of Demra's Staff Quarter area, and was used to transport employees of various offices.
Siddhirganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Emdadul Haque said police were working to identify those responsible. Further details would be shared after the investigation.

item.title: Moulvibazar temperature drops to 15.2°C as winter sets in
item.description:
Winter is beginning to set in across Moulvibazar, with temperatures falling steadily over the past few days and light fog covering tea gardens and haor areas in the early morning.
The minimum temperature in Sreemangal was recorded at 15.2°C at 9am on Wednesday, according to the Sreemangal Weather Observation Centre.
The centre's Officer-in-Charge Md Anichur Rahman said temperatures could drop further in the coming days.
Cold breezes have been felt since early morning and after sunset, particularly in tea garden areas.
Markets across the district have also started seeing increased sales of winter clothing.

item.title: PM provides Tk3cr grant to Christian community for Christmas
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday handed over a cheque for Tk3 crore in grants to representatives of the Christian community ahead of their biggest religious festival, Christmas.
The Prime Minister handed over the cheque at the Secretariat, said his Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin.
The grant has been increased by Tk1 crore from last year's allocation of Tk2 crore.
Tarique approved the increased amount to support the Christian community in celebrating Christmas, which marks the birth of Jesus Christ.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and Ethnic Communities Bijon Kanti Sarkar, MP and Senior Vice-Chairman of the Christian Religious Welfare Trust Anna Minj, and its Vice-Chairman Advocate John Gomes, among others, attended the cheque handover ceremony.

item.title: Portugal beat Wales to restore order after Ronaldo furore
item.description:
Portugal shrugged off a spirited Wales and the distraction of Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement with a 3-2 win in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League Group A4.
Bruno Fernandes, Pedro Neto and Carlos Forbs struck for Jorge Jesus's side as they bounced back from a 4-1 thrashing on home soil by Denmark on Saturday.
That result brought Ronaldo's decision to bring down the curtain on a 23-year international career after a falling out with Jesus back into focus.
But Portugal have won five of their six matches since Jesus took charge at the end of the World Cup.
Wales, already assured of finishing bottom of the table, made the worst possible start.
Joao Neves robbed Josh Sheehan and teed up Manchester United captain Fernandes to blast into the top corner on 11 minutes.
The lead lasted barely over a minute as David Brooks steered into the far corner after Harry Wilson's initial effort was repelled by Diogo Costa.
Portugal dominated possession but continued to give up huge chances to Wales on the counter-attack with Wilson denied once more by Costa.
Sorba Thomas then sprinted from inside his own half to give Craig Bellamy's side the lead from Brooks's through ball.
This time it was Wales who could not hold out as Neto pounced to level at the back post.
On an eventful night for the Chelsea winger, Neto then hit the post after a brilliant solo run.
Substitute Forbs proved to be the match winner with his first international goal after latching onto a poor headed clearance from Ben Cabango.
The visitors were forced to see out the final 15 minutes a man down after Neto was booked for two wild challenges barely two minutes apart.
Portugal, though, held on to bring some relief to Jesus, who was peppered with questions in the pre-match press conference over criticism from Ronaldo's mum Dolores Aveiro.
Portugal will face one of the Netherlands, Belgium or Spain in the last eight in Friday's quarter-final draw.
Norway also made the last eight after coming from 2-0 down to beat Denmark 3-2 and snatch second spot in the group thanks to a better head-to-head record.

item.title: Last-gasp Haaland shoots Norway into Nations League quarters
item.description:
Erling Haaland fired Norway into the Nations League quarter-finals on Tuesday with a last-gasp penalty which completed a stunning comeback from two goals down to win 3-2.
Manchester City striker Haaland stroked home from the spot in the sixth minute of injury time in Copenhagen as Norway leapfrogged their hosts into second place in Group A, on head-to-head record as both teams finished on nine points.
Both teams ended the group stage six points behind winners Portugal, who got their first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era with a 3-2 success against Wales.
The winner was one of two goals from Haaland, who also started the fightback in the 37th minute -- and had a goal disallowed -- after early strikes from Rasmus Hojlund and Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg gave Denmark a commanding lead in front of passionate support.
Haaland was given the chance to nick a spot in the last eight from the Danes, who only needed a draw to go through, after a handball from Joachim Andersen which was spotted by the VAR officials just as the hosts thought they had survived another in a series of scares.
Denmark had been on the back foot ever since Haaland halved the deficit when a howler from Denmark goalkeeper Mads Hermansen gifted possession to Martin Odegaard.
It was Odegaard who forced home Norway's leveller with six minutes remaining and set up a grandstand finish which was completed with Haaland's dramatic winner.
"This has been one of the craziest years in football I've ever experienced," said a relieved Haaland to TV2 in Norway.
Norway will join Portugal in Friday's draw in Nyon, where the four group winners will be seeded and each play against one of the four second-placed teams.
Haaland's winner made Portugal's win over Wales irrelevant to their group placing, but Carlos Forbs' classy strike in the 70th minute in Cardiff made sure of a positive finish for Jorge Jesus' team.
Forbs' first international goal decided a hugely entertaining encounter in which Wales, already guaranteed to finish bottom of the group, put in a performance which belied their position.
Wales will take part in the play-offs to decide the final promotion and relegation spots between Leagues A and B, and on Tuesday's evidence they have a fighting chance of staying in the top tier.
David Brooks quickly replied to Bruno Fernandes' superb opener for Portugal and Wales had their tails up when Sorba Thomas slid the hosts in front in the 40th minute.
But Pedro Neto, who was later sent off, almost immediately levelled the scores and Forbs decided an even contest and ensured Portugal would bounce back from a humiliating defeat at the hands of Denmark at the weekend.
"It's a special feeling; I won't forget today. The most important thing is that we managed to win," said Forbs.
"We needed the goal to calm the game down, and it just so happened that I scored."
Northern Ireland were promoted to League A for the first time after Justin Devenny's thumping strike gave his team the draw they needed against Hungary in Budapest.
Devenny, who plays for Stoke City in England's second tier, lashed home a beautiful strike in the 65th minute at the Ferenc Puskas Arena to level the match at 1-1 and secure a second successive promotion for Michael O'Neill's team.
"I feel amazing. I'm due one, that was my second for Northern Ireland. To see the game out, we dug deep and we've deserved it. We've had a great campaign and we can't wait for more," said Devenny to the BBC.
Republic of Ireland will join Wales in the play-offs after closing out Group B3 with a 3-0 win over 10-man Kosovo and moving into second place.

item.title: Paz at the double as Argentina thrash Costa Rica
item.description:
Rising star Nico Paz scored a superb double as Argentina bounced back from defeat with a 7-0 thrashing of Costa Rica in a friendly on Tuesday.
Italy-based Como attacking midfielder Paz -- who has emerged as a reported transfer target for incoming Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino -- underscored his talent with two spectacular first-half goals in Cordoba.
The 22-year-old, who scored twice in Como's 4-1 Champions League drubbing of United last month, lashed in Argentina's opener after just eight minutes at the Mario Alberto Kempes Stadium.
After Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez doubled Argentina's lead in the 35th minute, Paz then grabbed his second with the goal of the game.
Picking up the ball in midfield, the young forward held off the attention of several Costa Rican markers before twisting and turning into space inside the penalty area and crashing a shot into the top corner to make it 3-0.
Alvarez put Argentina into a 4-0 lead in the 43rd minute, beating Costa Rica goalkeeper Patrick Sequeira at the near post with a vicious shot that flew into the roof of the net.
Paz's virtuoso first-half performance was the highlight of a one-sided encounter as Argentina bounced back from suffering a 2-1 defeat to Uruguay in Buenos Aires on Friday.
Paz was substituted at half-time by Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni for Franco Mastantuono, the 19-year-old Fiorentina forward.
Like Paz, Mastantuono is another member of Argentina's next generation of young talent as the former world champions rebuild following the retirement from international football of Lionel Messi.
Mastantuono was quick to make his own mark on Tuesday's friendly, scoring just three minutes after coming on at half-time to make it 5-0.
Liverpool's Alexis Mac Allister swept in a sixth goal in the 78th minute before Mastantuono grabbed his second of the night two minutes from time with a thumping low strike.

item.title: Pochettino wraps US reign with 2-0 Haiti win, heads to Manchester
item.description:
Mauricio Pochettino's reign as United States coach ended with a simple 2-0 win over Haiti on Tuesday, sent off in style by a Christian Pulisic bicycle kick as he heads to his new role at Manchester United.
Teenager Julian Hall also added his fifth goal from six games to secure an 8-0 aggregate victory in the CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final second leg in Cincinnati, with Pochettino set to fly to England just hours after the final whistle.
Pochettino, who steered the US to the last-16 of a home World Cup this summer, picked a strong lineup for his swansong and his favored stars appeared determined to wave their coach off with a win, beginning with high intensity.
A bright Weston McKennie missed two good early chances, before turning creator in the 25th minute for Pulisic's opener.
Pulisic stole possession on the halfway line and surged up the left flank before feeding the ball inside.
McKennie crossed back into the box from the right and Pulisic, running away from goal, improvised a bicycle kick over his left shoulder that bounced in off the far post.
Teenage striker Julian Hall doubled the lead in the 43rd minute. McKennie again provided the assist, chipping the ball over the Haitian backline.
Hall did well to trap the ball, chest it down and then lift it over the goalkeeper. The 18-year-old has scored on all four US starts.
After the break Auston Trusty had a header acrobatically cleared off the line by Martin Experience. Video replays seemed to show it crossing over, but no goal was awarded.
Defensive midfielder Sebastian Berhalter picked up a yellow for a sliding challenge that rules him out of the semi-final in March.
Alex Freeman, the 22-year-old defender given his debut by Pochettino who has become a stalwart at right-back, did superbly to intercept a clear-cut chance for Josue Casimir.
Hall's header in the final few minutes bounced off the crossbar.
The often emotional Pochettino, who had issued a message before the game thanking US fans "from the bottom of my heart", calmly applauded Pulisic's spectacular strike, before exchanging warm hugs and smiles with his staff at the final whistle.
More testing challenges lie ahead, with United languishing in 18th place in the Premier League and due to face bitter rivals Liverpool on Sunday.
Pochettino is expected to head directly to United's Carrington training facility on arrival.

item.title: India comeback from behind against Pakistan to win record-extending 10th SAFF title
item.description:
India came from behind beat arch-rivals Pakistan 2-1 and clinched their record-extending 10th SAFF Championship title, becoming the first team to win the regional crown for a third consecutive time at the National Stadium here today.
Sandip Mandi struck an 88th-minute winner to break Pakistan's resistance after Suhail Ahmad Bhat restored parity following Junaid Shah's second-half dismissal.
Pakistan, appearing in their maiden SAFF final, looked on course for a historic triumph after taking a 1-0 half-time lead through Alamgir Ghazi's stoppage-time strike.
Both teams started aggressively, but Pakistan looked more threatening in the opening exchanges, repeatedly testing India's defence with their pace and attacking movements.
India threatened first in the fourth minute when Suhail Bhat broke into the Pakistan penalty area down the left flank after collecting a midfield pass, but his right-footed effort from the edge of the box sailed over the crossbar.
Pakistan responded with a flurry of attacks in the 17th minute, creating three successive scoring opportunities but failed to find the target, with Indian goalkeeper Arsh Shaikh comfortably gathering Aroon's weak effort.
India came close to breaking the deadlock in the 34th minute when a counterattack sparked a scramble inside the Pakistan box. The ball eventually fell to Ricky Shabong, whose effort was brilliantly kept out by Pakistan custodian Yousuf Butt.
Just when the first half appeared destined to end goalless, Pakistan struck in stoppage time. Junaid Shah's attempt took a deflection off Khaiminthang Lhungdim before falling kindly to Alamgir Ghazi, who calmly placed the ball into the net to give Pakistan a precious advantage heading into the break.
After the resumption, Pakistan were reduced to ten men in the 59th minute after Junaid Shah was sent off following a VAR review for a reckless challenge from behind on India's Brison Deuben.
The referee initially allowed play to continue without taking any action, but VAR intervened and recommended a review, resulting in a red card for the Pakistan midfielder.
The dismissal proved a turning point as India immediately capitalised on their numerical advantage. Awarded a free-kick for the foul, India restored parity in the very next minute when Suhail Bhat unleashed a superb strike to make the score line 1-1.
With extra time looming, India finally found the breakthrough in the 88th minute. Abdul Rabeeh delivered a corner into the Pakistan penalty area, and Sandip Mandi rose above the defence to direct a powerful header into the net.
The triumph marked India's 10th SAFF Championship title, extending their dominance in the regional competition. They had previously won the tournament in 1993, 1997, 1999, 2005, 2009, 2011, 2015, 2021 and 2023.
For Pakistan, it was a heartbreaking end to a historic campaign after reaching the final for the first time.
State Minister for Youth and Sports Md Aminul Haque was the chief guest at the prize distribution ceremony and handed over the trophy to the winners'.

item.title: Hasan, Taskin strike before rain washes out two sessions on Day 3
item.description:
Bangladesh fought back with three wickets in the opening session before persistent rain and thunderstorms forced an early end to the third day of the first Test against South Africa at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg on Tuesday.
South Africa reached 386-7 in 90 overs at stumps, trailing Bangladesh's first-innings total of 400 by just 14 runs, with only one session of play possible due to adverse weather conditions.
Resuming the day at 287-4, the hosts looked well placed to take control of the contest as captain Temba Bavuma and Ryan Rickelton continued their resistance. The pair added valuable runs before Bavuma was forced to retire hurt on 49 due to muscle cramps, with South Africa on 358-4.
Bangladesh, however, made the most of the second new ball to turn the momentum around. Taskin Ahmed struck twice in quick succession, first dismissing Wiaan Mulder for a duck before removing Marco Jansen for eight.
Hasan Mahmud then strengthened Bangladesh's position by dismissing Simon Harmer, leaving South Africa seven wickets down and still behind.
Rickelton remained unbeaten on 56 at the interval, while Kagiso Rabada was not out on five. Hasan was Bangladesh's most successful bowler, finishing with figures of 4-72, while Taskin claimed 2-88.
Bangladesh had earlier posted a formidable 400 in their first innings, built around Liton Das's century. The wicketkeeper-batter's innings provided the foundation for the visitors to put up a challenging total in the opening innings.
The second session was completely washed out as a severe thunderstorm, accompanied by heavy rain and hail, swept across Johannesburg. Although the rain briefly eased, persistent lightning, dark skies and further showers prevented the players from returning to the field after lunch.
There was little improvement in conditions ahead of the scheduled final session, with the ground remaining covered as thunder and lightning continued in the area. With no prospect of a resumption, the umpires eventually called stumps at around 3:55pm local time.
The weather interruption means South Africa will resume on the fourth morning needing just 14 runs to erase Bangladesh's first-innings advantage, with three wickets remaining. Rickelton's presence at the crease gives the hosts a chance to move ahead, while Bangladesh will look to wrap up the innings quickly and secure a potentially crucial first-innings lead.
Further rain is also forecast for the fourth day, raising the possibility of more interruptions in a match that remains finely balanced.

item.title: When books disappear, intolerance takes over
item.description:
A society does not become chaotic overnight. Its descent into intolerance, hostility, and disorder often begins much earlier, through small but consequential changes in the way people think, communicate, and understand one another.
One such change is the gradual disappearance of the habit of reading. In Bangladesh, where political disagreements increasingly turn into personal hostility, differences of opinion become grounds for confrontation, and public discussions frequently collapse into accusations and counteraccusations, the declining culture of reading deserves far more attention than it receives.
The absence of books from everyday life is not merely an educational deficiency or a cultural inconvenience. It can become a serious social and political liability.
Reading is often treated as an individual intellectual exercise, something people pursue for academic achievement, professional development, or personal entertainment. Yet its social significance extends considerably further.
Books expose readers to unfamiliar experiences, competing arguments, historical realities, and moral complexities. They encourage people to remain with an idea long enough to understand it before accepting or rejecting it.
A society that gradually loses this capacity risks producing citizens who are increasingly confident in their opinions but progressively less capable of examining them. The consequences become visible not only in classrooms but also in families, workplaces, political institutions, and public spaces.
Consider the difference between encountering an argument through a book and encountering it through a social media post. The former generally demands patience, concentration, and engagement with an extended line of reasoning. The latter often delivers conclusions without context, rewards immediate reactions, and encourages emotional identification with particular positions.
Neither medium is inherently incapable of informing people, but their effects depend considerably on how they are used. When short-form digital content becomes the principal source of knowledge, people may gradually lose the patience required to distinguish between evidence, interpretation, speculation, and manipulation.
Complex social problems are consequently reduced to simplistic explanations, while complicated human disagreements become contests between supposedly good and evil individuals.
This intellectual impatience has serious implications for a country like Bangladesh, where political and social divisions are already deeply embedded in public life.
Disagreement is a natural feature of any democratic society. Indeed, democracy cannot function without disagreement. The problem begins when people lose the ability to accept that someone can hold a different opinion without necessarily being ignorant, immoral, or hostile.
Reading literature, history, philosophy, and political thought can help cultivate precisely this understanding. By introducing readers to different historical periods, cultures, ideologies, and human experiences, books challenge the assumption that one's own perspective represents the entirety of reality.
John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty , defended the importance of allowing competing opinions to confront one another because even an erroneous opinion could contain part of the truth. His argument remains particularly relevant in a society where disagreement is frequently interpreted as disloyalty.
A reading culture does not automatically produce tolerant citizens, but it creates opportunities to encounter arguments that challenge existing beliefs. Without such encounters, convictions can harden into unquestionable assumptions, and public discourse can become increasingly hostile.
The relationship between reading and social acceptance is equally important. Literature allows individuals to enter lives vastly different from their own. A reader can experience the anxieties of a marginali z ed person, the desperation of someone living in poverty, the dilemmas of a political dissident, or the frustrations of an individual belonging to an unfamiliar community.
This imaginative engagement does not guarantee empathy, but it expands the possibility of understanding. As Atticus Finch observes in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird , one cannot truly understand another person without considering things from their perspective. The literary lesson is simple but profound: A cceptance begins when people become willing to imagine experiences beyond their immediate surroundings.
Bangladesh's declining interest in recreational reading should therefore concern us beyond the boundaries of education policy. A January 2025 study, Recreational Book Reading Among Secondary School Students in Bangladesh: Access, Trends and Issues , found that although 87% of participating students considered leisure reading important, only 38% actually read books outside their textbooks.
Another international survey published by CEOWorld Magazine in 2024 placed Bangladesh 97th among 102 countries in reading habits, estimating an average of 2.75 books per person annually.
These figures should be interpreted with an understanding of their methodological limitations, but they nevertheless raise important questions about the country's relationship with books.
The problem is not simply that young people are reading fewer novels or storybooks. It is that the educational environment often teaches them to regard knowledge as something to be acquired for examinations rather than explored for intellectual satisfaction.
A student who spends years memori z ing information without developing curiosity may eventually become a graduate who possesses certificates but struggles to engage critically with unfamiliar ideas. When education becomes primarily a process of reproducing approved answers, independent thinking becomes an unintended casualty.
The consequences can be particularly damaging in the political sphere. Political manipulation thrives where people lack the habit of questioning information, examining historical contexts, and evaluating competing claims. An uninformed public is not necessarily an unintelligent public, but it can become more vulnerable to deliberate misinformation.
When political narratives are consumed without scrutiny, rumours acquire the appearance of facts and collective anger can be directed towards convenient targets. The distance between disagreement and hostility consequently becomes dangerously short.
Gustave Le Bon's The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind examined how individual reasoning can become submerged in collective emotional behaviour. Although his arguments should not be treated as a complete explanation of contemporary mass psychology, they offer a useful reminder that crowds can become susceptible to suggestion and emotional contagion.
In Bangladesh, where social media can transform an allegation into a nationwide controversy within hours, the ability to pause, verify, and think independently is an essential civic responsibility. Reading cannot eliminate mob behaviour, but an intellectually curious population is better equipped to question the narratives that provoke it.
There is another dimension to this crisis: T he declining capacity to resolve conflicts through language. Reading develops vocabulary, but its deeper contribution is the ability to articulate disagreement without immediately resorting to aggression.
People who encounter diverse arguments and literary representations of human conflict become familiar with the possibility that opposing positions can contain legitimate concerns. They learn that persuasion requires more than volume, authority, or intimidation. In a society where public arguments increasingly resemble verbal combat, the ability to express disagreement constructively is itself a form of social capital.
Albert Camus, in The Plague , explores how ordinary people respond to collective suffering and moral responsibility. The novel reminds readers that social crises are not overcome through slogans or declarations of righteousness but through sustained responsibility towards others.
Such literature can help cultivate a moral imagination that extends beyond personal interests and political affiliations. This is particularly important in Bangladesh, where the language of collective welfare is frequently invoked but the practi c e of respecting differences remains inconsistent.
Of course, it would be simplistic to blame the country's social tensions entirely on declining reading habits. Economic inequality, unemployment, institutional weaknesses, political polari z ation, inadequate education, and the erosion of public trust all contribute to instability.
Nor does reading necessarily make someone compassionate or morally responsible. History contains enough examples of educated individuals participating in oppression and violence. Books can be misused, selectively interpreted, or turned into instruments of ideological indoctrination.
The real issue, therefore, is not merely how many books people read but whether society encourages independent, critical, and reflective engagement with knowledge.
That responsibility cannot rest exclusively on individuals. Families must create environments where children encounter books as sources of pleasure rather than additional academic burdens. Educational institutions need to move beyond examination-centred instruction and introduce meaningful reading programmes.
The state and local governments should consider public libraries, affordable books, and neighbourhood reading initiatives essential investments in social development. Publishers, writers, and educational institutions also have a responsibility to make books more accessible to readers throughout the year rather than depending excessively on the annual book fair.
A reading culture is not simply about producing more writers, academics, or literary enthusiasts. It is about developing citizens capable of thinking beyond immediate emotions, recogni z ing the humanity of people with whom they disagree, and questioning the assumptions that shape their understanding of the world.
A society that does not read may still produce graduates, professionals, and political leaders, but it risks losing the intellectual resources necessary to sustain meaningful coexistence.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: Who looks after the children of the industrial communities?
item.description:
Every day, parents across Bangladesh’s industrial hubs leave home to work in factories. For those with young children, one of the daily challenges is finding a safe place for their children to stay while they are at work.
For a young child, a parent’s long working day can mean staying with an older sibling, a relative or another informal caregiver, sometimes without adequate adult supervision.
Parents carry this worry with them to work, knowing that their children may not have access to the care and support they need. For children, the consequences can extend beyond safety to missed opportunities for early learning and greater exposure to other risks.
Bangladesh has invested heavily in industrial infrastructure over the past few decades, but the social infrastructure surrounding many industrial communities has not developed at the same pace.
We need to consider whether the well-being of workers and their children should be part of how we think about industrial development, rather than a separate social issue outside the factory gate.
My experience working with communities around industrial areas has increasingly convinced me that it should.
In the densely populated worker settlements of Mirpur in Dhaka and Kashimpur in Gazipur, an initiative supported by the Garcia Foundation, associated with Dutch enterprise JOG Group BV, brought Terre des Hommes Netherlands and Breaking the Silence, a Bangladesh based non-government organization, together to strengthen child protection at community level. The initiative responded to concerns about the care, early learning, and protection available to young children while their parents worked long hours in garment factories.
Community-based early childhood development (ECD) centres were one part of the response which provided children aged four to six with four hours of early learning, care, and basic safety awareness. They also helped prepare children for the transition to formal primary education. These were not full-day daycare facilities, and they did not cover the entire period when parents were at work. Their significance lay in the role they played within a wider effort to strengthen child protection in the surrounding communities.
The centres provided a trusted point of contact through which families could engage with broader community-based child protection activities. By connecting families, community structures, and wider child protection services, the initiative sought to build a system that could help communities recognize risks, respond to them, and create safer environments for children.
This experience raises a broader question: Could similar approaches work in other industrial communities in Bangladesh? Children are part of the industrial ecosystem even when they are outside the factory. Their well-being matters to families and communities, while parents may find it harder to concentrate on their work. Addressing these concerns requires us to look beyond the factory floor and consider the conditions in which workers’ families live.
An ECD centre cannot address every need, and a four-hour program cannot cover a parent's entire working day. Children may still face barriers to education, health, and social services, as well as risks of neglect or exploitation. The challenge is not simply a lack of services, but also the gaps between the people and institutions responsible for supporting children.
We are exploring this approach in another industrial setting through an emerging opportunity involving another Dutch enterprise, Royal LC Packaging, and their partner, Dutch Bangla Pack in Gazaria, Munshiganj. The intention is not simply to establish an ECD facility, but to explore a broader community-based child protection approach informed by the experience of the Garcia Foundation-supported initiative in Mirpur and Kashimpur.
Depending on local needs, this could involve engaging parents, strengthening community protection mechanisms, creating opportunities for children and young people to participate, and connecting families with relevant services.
The approach should not be replicated unchanged. Industrial communities differ in their needs, existing services, and relationships with employers and government. Any response must reflect these local realities while bringing families, communities, employers, civil society organizations, and public services together around children's needs.
This experience also raises questions about how companies and philanthropic organizations invest in communities. Rather than starting with a particular project, they could begin by asking what prevents children and families from getting the support they need.
In one community, the priority may be early childhood services; in another, it may be stronger protection mechanisms, support for parents, or better access to government services.
Corporate and philanthropic funding can help bring actors together, test approaches, and generate evidence. But these efforts should not create parallel systems that depend indefinitely on a single donor or company.
Employers can contribute resources and support workers and their families. Civil society organizations can provide expertise and maintain community relationships. Parents, young people, and local leaders can help identify risks and shape responses.
The government retains responsibility for protecting children's rights and providing public services. These roles should complement one another, with the aim of building arrangements that can continue beyond an individual project's funding period.
Bangladesh could test this approach in a small number of industrial communities where all concerned parties are willing to work together. The results should be assessed not only by the services established, but also by whether children are safer, families can access support, and community protection mechanisms are stronger. This should include examining what children need beyond ECD centre hours, so that future investment responds to the realities of workers' families.
Bangladesh’s industrial growth has created enormous economic opportunities, but the communities that sustain this growth need better support. They are places where children grow up, families make decisions, and the next generation is shaped. If we want these communities to be productive, resilient, and inclusive, we need to pay greater attention to the social infrastructure around them.
The opportunity is to build stronger connections between children, families, communities, employers, and public services so that the benefits of industrial growth extend beyond production and into people’s lives.
The factory gate should not be the boundary of our thinking about workers, their families, and their children. It should be the starting point.
Nazrul Islam is the Country Manager for Bangladesh and Partnership Specialist for Bangladesh and Thailand at Terre des Hommes Netherlands. Email: n.islam@tdh.nl .
